item.title: Who Gets to Be an Expert on Their Own Experiences?
item.description:
Addiction

Who Gets to Be an Expert on Their Own Experiences?

Not all of us are regarded as reliable sources of information about ourselves.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • People who struggle with addiction are often not regarded as reliable reporters on their own experiences.
  • Questions about addicts' abilities to be honest create a dangerous set of twinned stereotypes.
  • People in recovery may never be taken or respected as experts on their own recovery.

Can someone who has struggled with addiction be an expert on their own addiction and recovery? This may seem a puzzling question, but it is one that is emerging in the context of Brad Pitt’s announcement that he has decided to drink in a moderate or restrained way after seven years of being sober. His sobriety was in the context of Alcoholics Anonymous (AA), which makes it fair to assume that for him during that time, he abstained from alcohol.

Pitt’s decision is being second-guessed by many in different corners of the recovery world, most especially in Alcoholics Anonymous. Consider what Joe Schrank, a clinical social worker and person in recovery, offered in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter:

When he said he's drinking moderately after seven years of abstinence, there's a bunch of different things going on there. Typically speaking, alcoholics are just a horrible source of information about themselves. Matthew Perry walked around reeking like booze telling people he was sober.

The invocation of Matthew Perry to make his point is powerful; Matthew Perry died of an accidental ketamine overdose. Was Perry’s walking around telling people he was sober when he was reeking of alcohol evidence of his unreliability in self-reporting, or was it evidence that he was a liar?

Schrank conflates unreliability with lying, which happens quite frequently when it comes to people struggling with addiction. In Schrank’s view, it seems as if Perry’s lack of self-knowledge drove his lies. Or put slightly more charitably, Matthew Perry was so self-deceived that he couldn’t do anything but lie to himself and to others. By extension, Pitt may be doing the same thing.

What’s self-knowledge?

What does it mean to be a reliable source of information about yourself? This is the question of self-knowledge, which is one of the oldest questions in philosophy. One of the inscriptions at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi is “Know Thyself.” This is an exhortation or an appeal for each person to undertake the lifelong process of coming to know who they are.

While many philosophers took introspection to be the method of self-knowledge, others counseled looking both inwards and outwards. We humans are always works in progress who live within multiple social relations, act on commitments and projects, and navigate the hurly-burly of life. It is true that each of us can have some access to our own thoughts that others cannot (imagine those times you kept a straight face while laughing heartily on the inside), but this really isn't evidence for the self-knowledge at issue.

Much of our knowledge of ourselves comes from what we share with each other. We share experiences and come to know ourselves through them and in the company of others. I know myself because of how others experience and know me. Self-knowledge is relational and dynamic because that is what we humans are.

What is reliability?

Reliability is not just a trait or quality of a person; it is relational, though that is often ignored. If a person is an accurate and honest reporter of their self-knowledge but no one treats them as such, are they reliable? They are afforded no credibility. There’s a sticky wicket. To a significant degree, to be reliable and credible is to be treated as reliable and credible. At minimum, it is to have your claims and decisions taken seriously and not rejected out of hand.

Having decisions mocked or second-guessed because a person struggled with an addiction is par for the course. That is both unfair and harmful; it may be doubly so when other members of recovery communities and addiction and treatment professionals deploy those very stereotypes about unreliability and lying. Every time those stereotypes are deployed, they widen the credibility gap.

But what if someone is in AA?

Schrank does recognize that what Pitt is doing may be possible. He acknowledges:

The World Health Organization says that this is possible—that with moderate drinking, even after long periods of abstinence, there are lots of people who find success of clinical significance and life improvement. The AA morality police take this stuff as red meat for their need to finger wag and shame. Not everybody needs to spend the rest of their life totally abstinent with a cup of sh*tty coffee in a Styrofoam cup regurgitating platitudes. Some do—I'm one of those people.

Schrank appears to be distancing himself from others in AA but does so in a way that heralds his self-knowledge and knowledge acquired through years of working with people struggling with addiction. But why should we take him to be a reliable reporter on what he claims to know? This is not just some dodgy philosophical move: If he calls the knowledge-based authority of addicts in general into question, he doesn’t get to play the role of expert on his own or anyone else’s experiences.

This is a very undesirable conclusion. The way to avoid it is for all of us—people in recovery, treatment professionals, and others who love, live, and work with us—to stop trafficking in these dangerous stereotypes.

I am genuinely glad that Schrank knows what he needs, and I believe him. I choose to extend the same benefit to Brad Pitt.

item.title: Can Dogs Become Bilingual?
item.description:
Cognition

Can Dogs Become Bilingual?

Dogs can easily learn basic commands in more than one language.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • The average dog has the language ability of a 2 ½ year old child and can understand about 165 words.
  • In the USA and Canada combined, more than 85 million people live in bilingual households.
  • To function in an average household a dog needs to understand only about two dozen words for common commands.
  • It is possible to teach a dog to respond to more than one language.
Source: Bethany Ferr / Pexels

There has been a lot of interest in the ability of dogs to learn human languages, mostly focusing on spoken words, but sometimes including written words or symbols. I was recently giving a radio interview when a caller asked me if it was possible to teach her dog to become bilingual.

Here in Canada, where I live, approximately 18% of the population (about 6.6 million people) are bilingual in English and French. When you take into account all of the other languages (including immigrant and indigenous languages) roughly 41% of Canadians can conduct a conversation in more than one language.

Similarly, in the United States approximately 22% of people (more than 75 million) are bilingual. Of the 350 languages spoken in the US the most common second language is Spanish (representing about 66% of bilingual speakers). Other languages, each spoken by more than a million people include: Chinese (e.g. Cantonese and Mandarin), Tagalog (e.g. Filipino), Vietnamese, Arabic, and French.

Since in North America more than 25% of families own a dog, that means that a lot of dogs are living in a social environment where two or more languages are simultaneously in use. Is this a problem for our pets? Can they deal with multiple spoken languages in their home?

The Language Capacity of Dogs

My own research has led me to the conclusion that the language learning ability of the average dog is roughly equivalent to that of a human child aged 2 to 2 ½ years (roughly 165 words including signs and signals), while the language learning ability of a "super dog" (defined as members of those breeds of dogs in the top 20 percent of working and obedience intelligence) was roughly equivalent to a human child aged 2 ½ to 3 years (in excess of 250 words). This finding has been verified in several other studies in other laboratories.

Of course, there are savants or canine linguistic geniuses, like John Pilley’s Border Collie, Chaser, who had a demonstrated vocabulary of over 1000 words. But she was a special case, and Pilley intensively trained her several hours each day.

The Minimum Language Requirements for a Dog

In real life, the average dog only needs about two dozen words or phrases to get along in a household. Most of these are simple commands for action like: “come”, “sit”, “down”, “stay”, “no” or “stop”, and “leave it”. A couple of words of praise are useful, like “yes” or “good dog”. Practically a few place names come in handy, like, “go to your kennel” (or bed) or “go out”.

As is the case in even unilingual households, a specific command might have alternate vocal forms. For example, while I call my dog by saying “come”, my wife calls him by saying “here” and my granddaughter gets him to approach by calling “c’mere”. When I was still mobile enough to teach dog obedience classes an alternate way of calling him that I used was to simply announce “Your presence is required” which would cause my dog to come and sit in front of me.

The fact is that you can teach a dog to respond with any basic action as long as you are consistent in the words or phrases that you use, even if it is an alternate form to a previously learned command word and it does not matter whether the alternate command is in the same language or not. I just as well could have trained my dog to also respond to the French word “ici” (ee-see) or the Spanish word “ven” to ask him to come to me.

Training a Dog to Be Bilingual

When a human being wants to learn a second language they must learn not only the words, but grammar and syntax. For a dog all that is required is that they understand single words or phrases and respond to them, which means that teaching a dog to be bilingual is just as simple as teaching a dog to respond to alternative words in English that are associated with the same action.

If you have trained your dog using best practices, namely, in the early stages of teaching him you have combined the spoken command with a hand signal (like touching your left shoulder with your right hand when you say the word “come”), then teaching your dog to respond to a new label in a different language is easy. All you need to do is to combine the unfamiliar novel word with the familiar hand signal. Research has shown that hand signals are more consistently responded to than vocal signals, so the gesture drags the action out of the dog regardless of the unfamiliarity of the new sound. After a few repetitions, the new spoken word should suffice to produce the proper response from the dog, regardless of what language that spoken word comes from, even without the hand signal.

In the chart below I have listed 14 basic commands for dogs in English, with typical French and Spanish variants. This, combined with a bit of training using familiar hand signals should allow you to produce a functionally bilingual, or even trilingual, dog at least for basic household interactions.

item.title: What Does It Take for a Late-Life Marriage to Succeed?
item.description:
Relationships

What Does It Take for a Late-Life Marriage to Succeed?

Find out how to increase the odds of your “gray” relationship's survival.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Repartnering is increasingly common among older couples, especially with the rise in “gray divorce.”
  • As couples navigate their new partnerships, several factors may influence the nature of these bonds.
  • By learning more about the complexities of repartnering late in life, you can look ahead with optimism.

Marriage is perennially associated with young couples who, after some period of engagement and/or cohabitation, decide it’s time to make their relationship official. To be sure, the odds of a couple in their 50s or older deciding to head into marriage are not as high. However, with people living longer and deciding to end a failing relationship in their 50s (the “gray divorce”), there is increasing evidence that some aging couples decide to give a new partner a try. The question is, can these work and if so, how?

The Facts About Repartnering

According to a 2025 study by Bowling Green University’s Susan Brown and colleagues, not only is gray divorce increasing, but so are the numbers of 50+ divorced people who decide to try again. As many as 37 percent of men and 22 percent of women repartner after a late-life divorce, with the norm being cohabitation and the exception, marriage. People who want to be together at this point in life may feel they don’t need the formality of marriage.

You might think that people who decide to repartner are coming at this from the standpoint of putting it off as long as possible. Burned after their divorce, they may want to take time to contemplate their next steps before starting anew. There are, in fact, differences between men and women in this situation as well as differences in the choice to repartner based on prior marital history.

The men who want to repartner tend to have been married longer than women who want to try again. Also, men who were married more than once are also more likely to seek a third (or more) spouse. In general, heterosexual men have a wider range of potential new partners than do heterosexual women, due mainly to the lopsided sex ratio of male/females in later life because men have lower life expectancy.

A number of other gender-related factors also come into play. Older women aren’t as interested in repartnering, due to the “gendered bargain implied by remarriage and, to a lesser extent, cohabitation.” Women will be more likely to exchange household labor and caregiving for the men’s economic support. However, the trajectories of these go in opposite directions. Men will earn less after retirement, but will also need more care. Conversely, older men are less likely to want to commit to a woman who has her own caregiving responsibilities (perhaps to a parent). This piece of the puzzle can involve the children. If a man is close to his children, this could offset the caregiving problem because at least the kids can step in when needed.

Testing the Repartnering Process

Using the extensive dataset of the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), the authors identified 171 men and 78 women who repartnered, with 56 percent of women deciding to remarry compared to 40 percent of men. The key questions asked by the authors concerned the differences between those who remarried and those who cohabitated.

This comparison required that the research team control for the host of possible influences on couples in these situations. These included years of education, employment, home ownership, health, extent of social ties, and marital “biography” (duration of prior marriage, years since separation, age at separation, and then whether this was the first or later separation, and whether the separation involved divorce).

Beyond any effects of wealth, of the main findings to emerge from the comparison by gender of repartnering, it was marital biography that had the biggest impact. People who divorced were more likely to partner than those who were separated, and those who left a remarriage were more likely to make this decision. In line with life course theory, this suggests, in the words of the authors, that “earlier events and experiences have enduring consequences for subsequent transitions.”

It seems, then, that people lead with their heart rather than their heads in deciding to find a new partner. Even other possible factors besides wealth had no impact, at least for women (e.g., having children and grandchildren). It is possible that instead of relying on family, women rely on the friends in their social networks, which are broader than those of men.

You might be wondering what the dynamics are of a repartnered late-life union. For this, we turn to a 2022 study by University of Haifa’s Chaya Koren. This study, unlike Brown et al., included widowed late-life adults. Using an in-depth interview process of 38 couples, the U. Haifa authors zeroed in on the components of late-life love.

These older couples (ages 66 to 92) described love as a state of “feeling good,” divided into pleasant (not heated), parental (deep and quiet), and sibling (unity). As is true in all romantic relationships, repartnered love included being in love (in love like never before), partial love (feeling love, but sometimes), and falling out of love (but still caring for each other).

A key finding from the interview themes was that, unlike previous repartnering studies, participants reported their love to be exclusive: “Exclusivity in late-life repartnering pleasant love was found to be preserved by commitment, encompassing commitment and passion.” Unlike new relationships among younger partners, it was compassion rather than passion that seemed to most characterize the love held by these late-life individuals.

What to Expect From Repartnering

Putting these findings together, it appears that older couples who repartner do so not due to practical exigencies or even economic resources, but due to a desire to express warm feelings of love with the partner they regard as their one and only. Most importantly, as well, Koren concludes that whatever the view of the love in the relationship, it is shared by both partners.

New relationships can also be constructed in vastly different ways from prior ones, even though, as Brown et al. discovered, length of prior marriage predicted desire to repartner. As expressed by a participants in the U. Haifa study, “And I love him very, very much and he loves me like no one ever loved me like this, ever, it’s not because my husband didn’t love me, he didn’t know how to show it, he [my husband] was a completely different person, he [my partner] is an optimist.”

These studies, as comprehensive as they were, still leave open a number of questions that might come to your mind when you think about the practicalities of starting over in later life with a new partner. What happens to the house? What about all the permutations of children, stepchildren, grandchildren, and the entire cast of characters who make up an extended family? It seems that some of these stories have yet to be written.

To sum up, although some of the details remain undiscovered, the bottom line is that repartnering occurs in later life, and may be characterized, if not by passion, then by an exclusive sense of commitment and companionship. There’s much to look forward to if you hope to achieve fulfillment in late-life relationships, if not now, then in your future.
